An entry point asks what an observation means; the judgement itself is decided elsewhere so a second entry cannot answer differently.
A verdict is measured against recorded state, so policy reads snapshots and the runtime profile and never gathers them itself.

`scanner` runs every collector once per parsed module to build one `ScanResult`, and `report` also calls `violations.requires_violations` directly to judge the assembled contract without adding a second collector call inside the scanner.

`dart_scanner` assembles the Dart profile's observation from the libraries and import records `dart` reads, through the same shared record functions `scanner` uses for Python, so reading a Dart header and assembling an observation stay two jobs (AD-97).

`scanner` parses sources and builds the shared symbol index before handing parsed modules to the collectors, and both `scanner` and `report` write through the shared record envelope, so orchestration reaches the same foundation the collectors it calls already depend on.

Every collector reads a `ParsedModule` and writes through the shared `RawRecord`/`RawEvidence` envelope so a record from `bindings` and one from `symbols` compare the same way; `calls` and `references` also resolve names through the shared symbol index, which each would otherwise reimplement one call site at a time.
